title: Centring and opening porcelain clay
subtitle: Getting porcelain true on the wheel and opening without cracking the floor
excerpt: Porcelain is the most demanding clay body to centre and open on the wheel. It is denser than stoneware, has less plasticity, heats up quickly from hand friction, and collapses suddenly if overworked. This tutorial covers the specific adjustments needed to centre porcelain successfully and open it without cracking the floor: the two steps where most beginners working in porcelain fail.
sourceNotes: Porcelain-specific centering and opening methodology synthesised from studio ceramics throwing instruction. Porcelain properties and failure modes are documented across ceramics technical instruction literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: Pressing the clay particles together during throwing. Compression of the floor and base prevents S-cracks from forming during drying.
The process of bringing a ball of clay to the exact centre of a rotating potter's wheel, so that it runs true without wobble.

content.text: This technique requires a pottery wheel and applies to kiln-fired porcelain only. Porcelain fires to cone 8 to 10 (approximately 1260 to 1300 °C). Do not substitute air-dry clay: the technique described is specific to the mechanical properties of fire-clay porcelain bodies.
Before starting: prepare cold

Use porcelain straight from storage. Do not let it warm at room temperature for hours. Keep spare clay balls in a cool place. Use cold water for lubrication. Keep your hands cool if you can. Friction warms porcelain faster than stoneware and reduces the time you have for throwing.
Centring porcelain
Wet the wheel bat and slam the clay ball onto it firmly. For porcelain, a firm initial slam is more important than with stoneware: it ensures the clay adheres and does not lift during centring.

Run the wheel at medium speed (30 to 40 rpm). Place both hands on the clay: one compressing from above, one from the side. Apply less pressure than you would with stoneware: too much force creates surface tears and cracking in the outer clay layer. The goal is to coax the clay central with many light passes rather than force it in a few heavy ones.
Centring
is complete when the clay runs true with no lateral wobble. Check by resting your fingertip lightly against the spinning clay: at true centre there is no rhythmic deflection of your finger.

Keep the clay well lubricated throughout centring: porcelain absorbs water faster than stoneware in the early stages. Add water from a sponge whenever the surface looks dry. Dry porcelain during centring tears and creates surface weakness that propagates into cracks when pulling the walls.
Opening porcelain

Porcelain is less plastic than stoneware. It resists deformation more and cracks with less warning. Centring needs lighter pressure and more passes. When opening, compress the floor carefully to prevent S-cracks. Keep throwing sessions short. Porcelain warms from hand friction and becomes harder to work as the session goes on.

Open outward slowly and steadily, pressing toward the outer wall. Do not open in a single fast movement: porcelain tears if opened too quickly. Three slower passes outward are better than one fast pass.

Compress the floor thoroughly at the end of opening. This is the most important step for preventing S-cracks: press the flat of the thumb across the floor in a spiral from centre outward while the wheel turns slowly. Do this step twice.
Compression
aligns the clay particles and prevents the differential shrinkage that causes S-cracks through the floor during drying.

Check the floor is level using a needle tool: push the needle in at the inner edge of the floor while the wheel turns. If the needle drags unevenly, the floor has a lip or ridge. Level it with the thumb before beginning to pull walls.
Common mistakes
Clay surface tears during centring: too much pressure or dry surface. Slow down the pressure; add more water.
S-crack through the floor after drying: floor not compressed enough during opening. Compress the floor with thumb in spiral passes before pulling.
Clay becomes loose and sloppy partway through throwing: clay warmed up from friction. Stop. Set the piece aside to cool under a cloth, or return clay to fresh ball and restart on a cold piece.

rows.problem: Porcelain spirals during centring: clay has corkscrewed twist marks
rows.cause: Centring pressure applied in one direction only, not balancing from both sides simultaneously
rows.fix: Apply pressure with both hands simultaneously: one pressing down from above, one pressing inward from the side: rather than alternating between them.

rows.cause: Clay too cold and stiff; opened too quickly; or porcelain not properly wedged
rows.fix: Wedge more thoroughly. Warm the clay for 10 minutes in the hands before throwing. Open in three gentle stages rather than one movement.
